images.caption:
Peeblesshire's Coat of Arms Two of the salmon are swimming downstream, while the centre fish swims upstream: the Latin motto 'Contra Nando Incrementum' means 'There is increase by swimming against the stream', taking inspiration from the annual migration of the salmon up the Tweed. This plaque is situated in Northgate, though the three salmon symbol occurs in many places around the town.
(Source: 'Old Peebles' by Rhona Wilson, Stenlake Publishing 1998)
images.alt:
Peeblesshire's Coat of Arms Two of the salmon are swimming downstream, while the centre fish swims upstream: the Latin motto 'Contra Nando Incrementum' means 'There is increase by swimming against the stream', taking inspiration from the annual migration of the salmon up the Tweed. images.filename: Eastgate Theatre and Arts Centre, Peebles - geograph.org.uk - 598988.jpg
images.caption:
Eastgate Theatre and Arts Centre, Peebles The former Free Church (1871-72) in early Gothic style and prominent spire, marking the turning point of High Street towards its east end. Imaginatively adapted in 2003-4 as a theatre and arts centre, with a glazed screen acting as a frontispiece on the east side. Viewed from Tweedbrae.
(Source: Pevsner Architectural Guide, The Buildings of Scotland - Borders).

images.caption: Burgh School East. At the foot of School Brae there are two buildings which used to be educational establishments. This one has a panel carved with S Andrew's cross and was built in 1822 as the Grammar School - it has a side doorway engraved with the letter 'G'. An earlier building to the east of the same road-junction has a carving of three fishes, and was built in 1766 as the English School (see 1282989).

images.caption: Chambers House, Biggiesknowe, Peebles The white house is the birthplace of William (1800) and Robert (1802) Chambers, who went on to found the publishing company W&R Chambers in Edinburgh. Now a private house, sympathetically restored and maintained, it was open to the public on 5 September 2009 as part of the celebration of the 150th anniversary of the Chambers Institution in Peebles High Street.

images.caption:
Arthur's Seat, Edinburgh, viewed from Pollock Halls.  
1880s map of the park
Arthur's Seat, an extinct volcano and the highest point in Edinburgh, is at the centre of the park, with the cliffs of Salisbury Crags to the west. There are three lochs: St Margaret's Loch, Dunsapie Loch, and Duddingston Loch. The ruins of St Anthony's Chapel stand above St Margaret's Loch. Queen's Drive is the main route through the Park. St Margaret's Well and St Anthony's Well are both natural springs within the park. Holyrood Park is located to the south-east of the Old Town, at the edge of the city centre. Abbeyhill is to the north, and Duddingston village to the east. The University of Edinburgh's Pollock Halls of Residence are to the south-west, and Dumbiedykes is to the west.
Arthur's Seat is the remains of a now extinct volcano which rises 250 metres (823 feet) above Holyrood Park in Edinburgh.
